title: How to Develop Oracy
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues against building a stand-alone oracy curriculum, even though he admits that as an English teacher he is pre-programmed to love oracy. His thought experiment contrasts a student who writes and reasons well in formal language with one trained mainly in public speaking, and he claims the first becomes the better speaker anyway while the second costs the curriculum scarce study time. He backs this with Progress 8 figures for School 21, the flagship of the Voice 21 approach, which he says fell sharply over several years. The constructive half of the piece, taken from his book The Full English, shows how to build speaking into ordinary lessons through paired talk, random cold-calling, targeted vocabulary and the five connectives, so that oracy becomes preparation for writing. He ends with a rule-of-thumb critique of group work, which he says fails whenever students are learning something new and should be kept for applying knowledge already secured.
points: Oracy is best treated as a by-product of knowledge-rich reading and writing, so a separate oracy curriculum trades subject time for superficial confidence.
Scenario D shows that paired talk with short timers, teacher listening and random selection raises participation without needing a highly skilled questioner.
Having students speak a Because, Although, However, Therefore, Consequently chain before writing it forces them to build a linked argument.
Debate is offered as the way to build public speaking, but only when it is tied to a text or topic students will later write about.
Group work should be limited to applying secure knowledge, and the test is whether the task could be done as well in a pair or alone.
quotes: The second student robs Peter to pay Paul - since not all students can perform publicly at the same time, much study time will be lost while students practise their oral skills and others listen, or comment. This is likely to lead to worse progress in each subject overall.

But remember, the point of all your questioning is to find out what the students do and don’t know. So they need to answer in sentences to give you that correct feedback – do they know enough of what you have taught them?

The teacher is never looking for a right answer. Their default position is that the answer will always be underdeveloped. However, all students are likely to participate. They know that the teacher always listens to pairs as they talk, and this encourages them to talk about the task. They know that the teacher always picks a pair at random, so this also makes them want to talk in case they are the ones picked to explain to the class.
Because the connectives force students to link ideas, they are forced to create an argument, which inevitably leads to higher grade answers, regardless of the question format in the exam.
Oracy can easily be portrayed as a skill. I hope you have picked up that this book doesn’t really deal in skills as distinct from knowledge.
When does group work fail? Whenever you are asking students to learn something new. So most of the time!
Your golden rule is this: can it be done quicker or better in a pair or by a student on their own? The answer to this is nearly always in a pair, or on their own.
